name: Arikapú
confidence_why: The quoted passage has not been checked against the cited source.
catalog_citation: Ribeiro, Eduardo Rivail & Hein van der Voort. 2010. Nimuendajú was right: The inclusion of the Jabutí language family in the Macro-Jê stock. International Journal of American Linguistics 76(4): 517-570.
catalog_locator: Sec. 2.3.1.1 'Phonology' (under 2.3.1 'Arikapú'), p. 524, paragraph beginning 'The language also has diphthongs'; stress-marked forms pp. 524-525
catalog_quote: The language also has diphthongs, some of which contrast with combinations of multiple vowels that belong to different syllables, as in kaj ‘head’ vs. ka.i ‘hair, fur, feathers’. Stress is placed on the ultimate syllable of the word. The /j/ occurs also in onset position, in words like mujo ‘long club’, kuju ‘wing, feather’, rajo ‘uncle’. Furthermore, there are some cases of /j/-insertion in stressed syllables in certain words, such as kamə̃ ‘hill’ vs. kamə̃jtʃutʃɛ ‘on top of the hill’, kũ ‘grind’ vs. ihãkũj ‘grind seeds’, and inũtə̃(j)nõ ‘I’m sleeping’ (see table 2). [...] Word-internally, the preceding vowel is often nasalized, as in /kamu/ [kã·bu] ~ [kam·bu] ‘young one’; /kra-mrə/ [krã·brə] ~ [kra·mbrə] ‘beads’ (lit., ‘stone-little’) ([·] indicates stress placement).
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Arikapú is not in the catalog. The only title-keyword hit (Benus, Gravano & Hirschberg 2007, Interspeech, 'Prosody, emotions, and… whatever') is an American English intonation paper; Glottolog attached it to Arikapú by a computerized language code assignment from the title word 'whatever' — downloaded, read and saved, irrelevant, priority none. The genuine first-hand stress statements were already held by the project from an earlier reading and I re-read and re-verified them from the PDFs: Ribeiro & van der Voort 2010 IJAL p.524 'Stress is placed on the ultimate syllable of the word'; van der Voort 2007 p.138 'O acento principal da palavra está na última sílaba da raiz lexical'; Rosa Ribeiro 2008 sec. 2.3 p.16 'O acento tônico recai sempre na última sílaba da palavra'; plus a stress minimal pair (ütxi paroxytone 'aguar' vs oxytone 'secar') in the 2010 Vocabulário p.50. Recommended coding for a new catalog record: fixed final (root-final) stress with a noted lexical exception. the still-unlocated van der Voort 2005 'A descrição do Arikapú' (10 pp.) is not needed given the three first-hand statements already read.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Arikapú is fixed on the final syllable; van der Voort's own 2007 Portuguese sketch words it as the last syllable of the lexical root (so grammatical suffixes such as -nõ in inũtə̃(j)nõ apparently fall outside the stress domain), and Rosa Ribeiro 2008 independently states stress 'always' falls on the last syllable of the word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in any of the sources opened (van der Voort 2007 speaks of 'acento principal' but does not describe a secondary one).
new_statements.exceptions: IJAL 2010 and van der Voort 2007 state no exceptions; the 2010 Vocabulário (p.50) records one lexicalised paroxytone item, ütxi 'aguar' [ǘtxi] (lit. 'put water'), contrasting with oxytone ütxi 'secar' [ütxí]. The /j/-insertion example inũtə̃(j)nõ suggests the stressed syllable is root-final rather than word-final when a suffix follows, matching the 2007 'última sílaba da raiz lexical' wording.
new_statements.domain_note: IJAL 2010 says 'ultimate syllable of the word'; van der Voort 2007 p.138 says 'O acento principal da palavra está na última sílaba da raiz lexical' (last syllable of the lexical root) — same author, same 2001-2004 field data; person prefixes and proclitics are unstressed in all transcriptions (Rosa Ribeiro 2008: [(ə)tʃi(ə)'Ri] 'para ele'). Statements concern isolated words/citation forms; no phrase-level prosody described.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Arikapú proper (arik1265), based on the last two speakers (T.I. Rio Branco and T.I. Rio Guaporé, Rondônia), fieldwork 2001-2004 (van der Voort) and c. 2007 (Rosa Ribeiro, one speaker). No dialect differentiation. Sister language Djeoromitxí (djeo1235) is described in the same IJAL article with the same final-stress rule (p.531). The earlier scan's 'LIAMES 7' citation for van der Voort 2007 was wrong; the article is in Boletim do Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi, Ciências Humanas 2(2).

sources.note: Fonotaxe sec. 2.3, p.16: 'O acento tônico recai sempre na última sílaba da palavra.' with examples #pa'Raɪ# 'demolir', #ndiRi'Ri# 'tremer'; transcriptions throughout mark final stress (proclitic tʃi= and prothetic (ə) unstressed). Independent fieldwork (student of Henri Ramirez) with one of the last speakers.

sources.note: Section 'Características básicas da língua Arikapú', p.138 (p.6): 'O acento principal da palavra está na última sílaba da raiz lexical.' (main word stress on the last syllable of the lexical root); phonetic forms marked with final stress: [bi'ku] 'terreiro', [kã'bu] 'jovem', [krã'brə] 'miçanga', [dun'dɨ] 'peito'. (The earlier scan mis-cited this as LIAMES 7; it is in Bol. MPEG Ciências Humanas.)
